sources.title: VENTURE experiment result: publish-anomaly retrospective (pre-registered analysis)
sources.excerpt: Incidents with a new-dependency or install-hook signal: 58 of 58 classifiable (100.0%). … Legitimate consecutive releases that add a dependency or install script: 14 of 1119 (1.3%). … Verdict (pre-registered rule): supported: 100.0% of incidents carry a signal (≥ 60%) and 1.3% of legitimate releases do (< 10%).
sources.limitations: Own experiment. Mechanisms are classified by keyword rules over OSV report text. npm only.

sources.title: VENTURE experiment: independence check of incidents (not pre-registered)
sources.excerpt: 56 of the 60 analysed incidents were published on 2026-08-04 and their OSV reports attribute them to the same Shai-Hulud campaign wave. … Counted by campaign instead of by package, the sample contains about 5 independent attacks, far below the 15 the design intended. … Interpretation: the pre-registered verdict stands as recorded, but it rests mostly on one worm campaign whose payload used `preinstall` hooks. It shows that this campaign would have been caught by an install-hook diff with a low false-positive rate (1.3% of legitimate releases). It does not establish that hijacks in general carry such signals. The asyncapi compromise (2026-07-14, outside the newest-60 sample) modified an existing file and would not have triggered either signal.

evidence.claim: In the newest 60 hijacked npm packages in the OpenSSF dataset, 58 of 58 classifiable incidents carried a new install-hook signal, and only 1.3% of legitimate releases did.
evidence.quote: Incidents with a new-dependency or install-hook signal: 58 of 58 classifiable (100.0%).

evidence.claim: 56 of the 60 incidents come from one Shai-Hulud campaign wave, so the sample holds only about 5 independent attacks.
evidence.quote: Counted by campaign instead of by package, the sample contains about 5 independent attacks, far below the 15 the design intended.
evidence.context: Limits how far the supportive result generalises: it mainly shows that one worm campaign was detectable.

evidence.claim: A known hijack outside the sample (asyncapi) only modified an existing file, so it would not have triggered either signal.
evidence.quote: The asyncapi compromise (2026-07-14, outside the newest-60 sample) modified an existing file and would not have triggered either signal.

experiments.title: Campaign-level replication: do independent hijack campaigns carry structural signals?
experiments.hypothesis: Across independent npm hijack campaigns (not individual packages), most carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal.
experiments.uncertainty: Whether the first experiment's support generalises beyond the single Shai-Hulud wave that dominated its sample.
procedure: Pre-registered 2026-11-03, before any campaign-level data collection.
Population: OpenSSF OSV reports 2024-01-01..2026-11-02 for hijacked legitimate npm packages (at least 10 non-malicious versions).
Group incidents into campaigns: same campaign name in the report, or same publish date and payload description. Take one representative per campaign.
Classify each campaign's mechanism as in exp-publish-anomaly-retrospective. Reuse the same false-positive baseline method.
successCriteria: At least 60% of classifiable campaigns carry a new-dependency or install-hook signal, with at least 15 classifiable campaigns
failureCriteria: Fewer than 40% of classifiable campaigns carry such signals
experiments.estimatedTime: half a day of automated analysis
experiments.expectedLearning: Whether structural diffing generalises across attackers, or only catches worm-style campaigns.

nextSteps.ifSuccess: Survey vendor offerings for maintainer-side alerts, then prototype on VENTURE's own packages (none yet).
nextSteps.ifFailure: Narrow the idea to worm/install-hook detection or park it.
